    19	\section{At a glance}
    20	
    21	\begin{itemize}
    22	  \item \textbf{Difficulty.} Medium.  The source quotes a fiberwise consequence
    23	  of a state-dependent quantum linearity theorem, but suppresses two averages
    24	  and a compatibility argument for the auxiliary spaces.
    25	  \item \textbf{Estimated weight.} One faithful theorem for a single family,
    26	  followed by a finite common-extension construction that makes the auxiliary space
    27	  uniform over the outer parameters.
    28	  \item \textbf{Mathlib/project split.} Finite direct sums, extensions of
    29	  operators, and squared norms are standard linear algebra.  The imported
    30	  quantum linearity theorem and its state-dependent metric are project-level
    31	  inputs.
    32	  \item \textbf{Key mathematical inputs.} Theorem~10 of
    33	  \cite{Natarajan2017Linearity}, finite averaging, and extension by the identity
    34	  on orthogonal summands.  This reduction is tracked in
    35	  \ghissue{19}.
    36	\end{itemize}
    37	
    38	\section{Key theorem forms}
    39	
    40	Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, let $\rho$ be an arbitrary
    41	density operator on $H$, and let $u\mapsto O^u$ be binary observables on $H$,
    42	indexed by $\mathbb F_2^t$.  The cited theorem assumes the averaged
    43	correlation estimate
    44	\[
    45	  \mathop{\mathbb E}_{u,v}
    46	  \operatorname{Tr}\!\left(O^u O^v O^{u+v}\rho\right) \geq 1-\delta.
    47	\]
    48	It produces an auxiliary space $H'$, a unit vector $\mathrm{anc}\in H'$, and
    49	binary observables $L^u$ on $H\otimes H'$ satisfying, with
    50	$\rho'=\rho\otimes|\mathrm{anc}\rangle\langle\mathrm{anc}|$,
    51	\[
    52	  L^uL^v=L^{u+v}
    53	  \quad\text{for every }u,v.
    54	\]
    55	Moreover,
    56	\[
    57	  \mathop{\mathbb E}_{u}
    58	  \operatorname{Tr}\!\left((L^u-O^u\otimes I_{H'})^\dagger
    59	    (L^u-O^u\otimes I_{H'})\,\rho'\right)\leq\delta.
    60	\]
    61	In particular, $L^0=I$: exact linearity gives $(L^0)^2=L^0$, while an
    62	observable is invertible.
    63	
    64	The chapter needs a parameterized version.  For each pair $(x,z)$ it applies
    65	the theorem to $(r,s)\mapsto O^{x,z,r,s}$.  Since the provider theorem accepts
    66	the actual nonnegative defect on each fiber, no assumption that a fiber defect
    67	is at most one, and no good--bad fiber split, is needed.  One must still
    68	formulate the finite common-extension step that makes the auxiliary space
    69	uniform over $(x,z)$.
    70	
    71	\section{Comparison with the quoted statement}
    72	
    73	Lines~711--725 of
    74	\path{references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex} quote the
    75	linearity theorem.  The displayed hypothesis correctly averages over both
    76	group variables.  The displayed conclusion, however, says that the corrected
    77	observable is close for every $u$, whereas Theorem~10 of the cited work gives
    78	closeness only on average over $u$ \cite{Natarajan2017Linearity}.  The quotation
    79	also inserts $\delta\leq1$, which is absent from the provider theorem and would
    80	unnecessarily obstruct applying it with a fiber's actual defect.  The assertion
    81	at the identity follows from exact linearity as above.
    82	
    83	Lines~825--832 construct the family $O^{x,z,r,s}$ and establish approximate
    84	linearity only after averaging over $x,z,r,r',s,s'$.  They then apply the
    85	single-family theorem separately for every $(x,z)$ and state that sufficiently
    86	many zero ancillas avoid a further extension.  The remaining implicit step is
    87	to make the theorem's possibly fiber-dependent auxiliary spaces uniform.
    88	
    89	The finite setting admits a standard repair.  Apply the theorem on each fiber
    90	with its actual defect, choose one finite auxiliary space large enough for all
    91	returned spaces, and embed each returned space so that its unit vector maps to
    92	one fixed vector.  Extend the conjugated observables by the identity on the
    93	orthogonal complement.  The embeddings may depend on the fiber because the
    94	observables do.  Averaging then yields the conclusion used later in the
    95	chapter.  This is an open reduction, not a counterexample to the quoted theorem
    96	or to the source's eventual combined-measurement conclusion.
    97	
    98	\section{Blueprint and formalization status}
    99	
   100	The blueprint records the averaged theorem form and the common-ancilla
   101	obligation in
   102	\path{blueprint/src/chapter/ch15_qpbt_combining.tex}, lines~82--180.  No
   103	source-labelled Lean theorem should assert pointwise closeness or a common
   104	auxiliary space until that finite-family reduction has been proved.
   105	The chapter-16 extraction statements may consume the resulting global-pair
   106	witness once the reduction is discharged; they must not assume a new
   107	fiberwise linearity hypothesis.
   108	
   109	\section{Conclusion}
   110	
   111	The primary discrepancy is a quantifier mismatch in the quotation: the cited
   112	linearity theorem gives average, not pointwise, closeness.  Its use for the
   113	family indexed by $(x,z)$ also requires an explicit finite common-extension
   114	argument.  Both are open formal reductions compatible with the intended
   115	source conclusion.

    13	\author{}
    14	\date{2026-09-03}
    15	
    16	\begin{document}
    17	\maketitle
    18	
    19	\section{At a glance}
    20	
    21	\begin{itemize}
    22	  \item \textbf{Difficulty.} Medium.  The source applies a decoder--encoder
    23	  identity to every bounded individual-degree polynomial, although the identity
    24	  is guaranteed for encoded polynomials and can fail outside the encoding image.
    25	  \item \textbf{Estimated weight.} One restricted algebraic identity and one
    26	  probabilistic estimate showing that the constructed measurement assigns
    27	  little state-dependent mass to outcomes outside the encoding image.
    28	  \item \textbf{Mathlib/project split.} Evaluation of the multilinear
    29	  interpolant is elementary polynomial algebra.  The non-encoding-mass bound
    30	  uses project-specific consistency estimates and Schwartz--Zippel.
    31	  \item \textbf{Key mathematical inputs.} Multilinear interpolation on the
    32	  Boolean cube, injectivity of the low-degree encoding, measurement
    33	  consistency, and Schwartz--Zippel.  The correction is tracked in
    34	  \ghissue{19}.
    35	\end{itemize}
    36	
    37	\section{Key theorem forms}
    38	
    39	For a word $h\colon\{0,1\}^m\to\mathbb F_q$, let $g_h$ be its multilinear
    40	extension.  Define the chapter's decoder by
    41	\[
    42	  \operatorname{Dec}(g)(y)=g(y),
    43	  \qquad y\in\{0,1\}^m.
    44	\]
    45	Then
    46	\[
    47	  \operatorname{Dec}(g_h)=h
    48	  \quad\text{and}\quad
    49	  \operatorname{Dec}(g_h)\mathbin{\cdot}\operatorname{ind}_m(u)=g_h(u).
    50	\]
    51	More generally, the second identity holds for a polynomial outcome $g$ under
    52	the explicit hypothesis that $g$ belongs to the image of the encoding; no
    53	converse is asserted.
    54	
    55	For an arbitrary bounded individual-degree polynomial $g$, the Boolean values
    56	determine its multilinear interpolant, not necessarily $g$ itself.  The
    57	unrestricted identity
    58	\[
    59	  \operatorname{Dec}(g)\mathbin{\cdot}\operatorname{ind}_m(u)=g(u)
    60	\]
    61	is therefore false.
    62	
    63	\section{Counterexample and source comparison}
    64	
    65	The low-degree encoding is defined at lines~873--897 of
    66	\path{references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex}.  The general decoder at
    67	lines~917--924 retains evaluations lying in a chosen subset $H$; the extraction
    68	chapter instead specifies at lines~1419--1420 of
    69	\path{references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex} that the
    70	decoder returns all evaluations on the Boolean cube.  This is the specialization
    71	$H=\mathbb F_q$, rather than the Boolean-valued shorthand used earlier
    72	\cite[lines~873--924 and 1419--1420]{Ji2020MIPStar}.
    73	
    74	Take $m=1$, $d\geq2$, and a field of characteristic two with more than two
    75	elements.  For $g(x)=x^2$, the Boolean evaluations are $g(0)=0$ and $g(1)=1$.
    76	Consequently the decoder is the word whose multilinear extension is $x$.
    77	For any $u\notin\{0,1\}$ with $u^2\neq u$,
    78	\[
    79	  \operatorname{Dec}(g)\mathbin{\cdot}\operatorname{ind}_1(u)=u
    80	  \neq u^2=g(u).
    81	\]
    82	Thus the equality asserted for every $g$ at lines~1483--1492 of the chapter-14
    83	source mirror is false \cite[lines~1483--1492]{Ji2020MIPStar}.  If degrees at
    84	least $q$ are allowed, equality as a function would not by itself prove encoding
    85	membership either, since $x^q$ and $x$ induce the same function on $\mathbb F_q$.
    86	
    87	\section{Required repair}
    88	
    89	The extraction proof must split the marginal measurement into encoding and
    90	non-encoding outcomes.  On encoding outcomes, the restricted identity above
    91	justifies the substitution.  On the complement, the proof must bound
    92	\[
    93	  \sum_{g\ \mathrm{not\ an\ encoding}}
    94	  \langle\widehat\psi,\widehat S_g^W\widehat\psi\rangle.
    95	\]
    96	The blueprint derives an $O(\delta_S)+md/q$ bound from point consistency and
    97	the combined point measurement.  A non-encoding polynomial differs from every
    98	encoded polynomial, so Schwartz--Zippel bounds the probability that their
    99	evaluations coincide.  This estimate is the open reduction; it must be proved
   100	from the paper hypotheses rather than inserted as an extraction hypothesis.
   101	
   102	The conjugation calculation at lines~1805--1822 does not require the false
   103	unrestricted identity.  Its decoder term cancels against the outcome shift,
   104	and only linearity of $h\mapsto g_h$ and the genuine identity
   105	$\operatorname{Dec}(g_h)=h$ are needed
   106	\cite[lines~1805--1822]{Ji2020MIPStar}.
   107	
   108	\section{Blueprint and formalization status}
   109	
   110	The decoding-identity remark and the proof of the pulled-apart consistency
   111	lemma in
   112	\path{blueprint/src/chapter/ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex} state the restricted
   113	identity and isolate the non-encoding-mass estimate.  The Lean API should
   114	therefore require encoding membership at every use of the dot-product
   115	evaluation theorem.  No unrestricted theorem, residual assumption, or witness
   116	field is source-faithful.
   117	
   118	\section{Conclusion}
   119	
   120	The decoding identity is false for a general polynomial outcome.  Restricting
   121	it to the encoding image is a necessary local correction.  Recovering the
   122	source's measurement-consistency conclusion then requires the separate
   123	non-encoding-mass estimate, which remains an open proof obligation.

    18	
    19	\section{At a glance}
    20	
    21	\begin{itemize}
    22	  \item \textbf{Difficulty.} Low.  The source drops a nontrivial phase when the
    23	  two binary-basis indices are distinct.
    24	  \item \textbf{Estimated weight.} One exact multiplication calculation for
    25	  generalized Pauli observables; no robustness estimate changes.
    26	  \item \textbf{Mathlib/project split.} Finite-sum bilinearity and the field
    27	  trace are standard algebra.  The extracted-observable product form and the
    28	  project's phase convention are project-local.
    29	  \item \textbf{Key mathematical inputs.} The generalized Pauli commutation
    30	  relation and nondegeneracy of the trace pairing.  The local correction is
    31	  tracked in \ghissue{19}.
    32	\end{itemize}
    33	
    34	\section{Key theorem forms}
    35	
    36	Let $e_1,\ldots,e_t$ be the fixed self-dual basis of $\mathbb F_q$ over
    37	$\mathbb F_2$.  With the phase convention of the source, generalized Pauli
    38	observables satisfy
    39	\[
    40	  \tau^X(a)\tau^Z(b)
    41	  =(-1)^{\operatorname{tr}(a\mathbin{\cdot}b)}
    42	   \tau^Z(b)\tau^X(a).
    43	\]
    44	Substituting $a=e_j\widetilde u$ and $b=e_{j'}\widetilde v$ gives the exact
    45	relation
    46	\[
    47	  \widetilde X^j(\widetilde u)\widetilde Z^{j'}(\widetilde v)
    48	  =(-1)^{\operatorname{tr}
    49	      (e_je_{j'}(\widetilde u\mathbin{\cdot}\widetilde v))}
    50	   \widetilde Z^{j'}(\widetilde v)\widetilde X^j(\widetilde u).
    51	\]
    52	This formula applies uniformly, whether or not $j=j'$.
    53	
    54	\section{The false dichotomy in the source}
    55	
    56	Lines~1438--1450 of
    57	\path{references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex}
    58	identify each extracted observable with a tensor product containing
    59	$\tau^W(e_j\widetilde u)$.  Lines~1451--1456 then claim that the extracted
    60	$X$- and $Z$-observables commute whenever $j\neq j'$
    61	\cite[lines~1438--1456]{Ji2020MIPStar}.  Self-duality gives only
    62	\[
    63	  \operatorname{tr}(e_je_{j'})=0 \qquad (j\neq j').
    64	\]
    65	It does not imply
    66	\[
    67	  \operatorname{tr}(e_je_{j'}s)=0
    68	  \qquad\text{for every }s\in\mathbb F_q.
    69	\]
    70	
    71	Indeed, for distinct $j,j'$, the element $c=e_je_{j'}$ is nonzero.  The trace
    72	pairing is nondegenerate, so there is an $s\in\mathbb F_q$ for which
    73	$\operatorname{tr}(cs)=1$.  Taking vectors whose first coordinates are $1$
    74	and $s$, with all remaining coordinates zero, gives
    75	$\widetilde u\mathbin{\cdot}\widetilde v=s$.  The two extracted observables
    76	then anticommute.  This is a counterexample to the printed cross-basis
    77	commutation assertion.
    78	
    79	When $\widetilde u\mathbin{\cdot}\widetilde v$ lies in the prime field, the
    80	printed distinction is recovered from self-duality.  The chapter quantifies
    81	over arbitrary vectors, however, so that special case does not repair its
    82	statement.
    83	
    84	\section{Blueprint and formalization status}
    85	
    86	The discussion following the product-form calculation in
    87	\path{blueprint/src/chapter/ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex}, lines~69--95, records
    88	the full phase and notes that the false dichotomy is not used later in the
    89	extraction argument.  A formal theorem may therefore retain the mathematically
    90	correct uniform phase relation with a \textbf{Local fix} marker.  It must not
    91	assert exact commutation merely from $j\neq j'$.
    92	
    93	This correction changes neither the definition of the extracted observables
    94	nor the source-faithful consistency and extraction conclusions.  It repairs an
    95	auxiliary algebraic assertion that is independent of the robustness estimates.
    96	
    97	\section{Conclusion}
    98	
    99	The source's cross-basis commutation claim is false for general
   100	$\widetilde u$ and $\widetilde v$.  The correct relation retains the phase
   101	$(-1)^{\operatorname{tr}(e_je_{j'}(\widetilde u\cdot\widetilde v))}$.
   102	Because the later argument does not invoke the false dichotomy, this is a
   103	local correction rather than an additional hypothesis on the extraction
   104	theorem.

   213	The `issue-automation` workflow will automatically:

     2	
     3	The canonical convention documents live in the `lean-conventions` skill of
     4	[texra-ai/texra-lean-skills](https://github.com/texra-ai/texra-lean-skills)

    10	
    11	## Style (MATHLIB_style)
    12	
    13	### Linter warnings
    14	
    15	Do not mask linter warnings instead of fixing them. A cleanup PR should not add
    16	broad `set_option linter.<name> false` blocks, and especially not file-wide
    17	blocks, just to make the build output quieter. Linters exist to expose real
    18	maintenance problems; hiding them makes later proof work and review harder.
    19	
    20	Fix the warning at its source whenever possible:
    21	
    22	- wrap long lines rather than disabling `linter.style.longLine`;
    23	- remove or narrow unused variables, section variables, and unused typeclass
    24	  assumptions rather than disabling the corresponding unused-* linter;
    25	- remove unused `simp` arguments rather than disabling `linter.unusedSimpArgs`;
    26	- rewrite proof terms or state the simplified goal explicitly rather than
    27	  silencing `linter.flexible`.
    28	
    29	If a linter warning is a genuine false positive or a temporary porting
    30	exception, use the narrowest possible scope, preferably
    31	`set_option linter.<name> false in <decl>`, and add a short nearby explanation.
    32	Such exceptions should be rare and reviewable. Never use linter suppression as
    33	the main mechanism for a linter-warning cleanup PR.
    34	
    35	## PR review (MATHLIB_pr-review)
    36	
    37	### Source-faithfulness checks
    38	
    39	For this repository, the first review question is whether a paper-facing Lean
    40	statement still represents the cited result in `references/ldt-paper/`.  Before
    41	applying the general mathlib review checklist in the lean-conventions
    42	`MATHLIB_pr-review` reference, compare every changed
    43	source-labelled theorem, lemma, proposition, corollary, or definition with the
    44	corresponding paper statement and the active blueprint entry.
    45	
    46	Reject a paper-facing statement if it has acquired a non-paper bridge, residual,
    47	repair, package, producer, proof-obligation, assumptions-bundle, hypotheses-bundle,
    48	or arbitrary implication hypothesis.  Necessary boundary hypotheses, such as
    49	positivity for division or nonemptiness of a finite type, may be faithful formal
    50	encodings of implicit paper assumptions, but they should be documented when
    51	mathematically load-bearing.
    52	
    53	Reviewers should also inspect `\lean{}` and `\leanok` links.  A source-labelled
    54	blueprint entry should point to the source theorem or its faithful construction
    55	theorem, not to conditional helpers whose assumptions are proof obligations.
    56	Auxiliary Lean declarations may be recorded in a separate remark, provided the
    57	remark states that they are not additional hypotheses in the paper theorem.
    58	
    59	## Proof integrity (PROOF_INTEGRITY)
    60	
    61	### Companion document
    62	
    63	> **Companion document:** [`anti_patterns.md`](./anti_patterns.md) catalogues
    64	> subtler proof-evasion patterns that pass every blocker check in the
    65	> lean-conventions `PROOF_INTEGRITY` reference yet still
    66	> fail to prove the claimed mathematics (conclusion-shaped hypotheses,
    67	> definitional sleight-of-hand, zero-fallback branches, trivial default
    68	> witnesses, Mathlib-bypass castles, external `*Statement` smuggles).
    69	> Consult it alongside this file during review.
    70	
    71	### Project paper-realignment protocol
    72	
    73	The canonical paper-realignment exception in the lean-conventions
    74	`PROOF_INTEGRITY` reference is instantiated here as
    75	follows (the protocol and the `**Unfaithful:**` marker are described in
    76	`AGENTS.md`):
    77	
    78	> **Paper-realignment exception:** When a PR is explicitly realigning a
    79	> source-labelled declaration with `references/ldt-paper/`, the `sorry`
    80	> blocker of the lean-conventions `PROOF_INTEGRITY` reference may be
    81	> temporarily relaxed for the affected proof bodies.  The
    82	> PR must restore the source-faithful public statement, name the remaining proof
    83	> obligation as a theorem or lemma, and cite the paper passage plus the
    84	> tracking issue or paper-gap note.  A theorem whose proof still depends on a
    85	> known non-paper bridge, residual, repair input, obligation structure, or
    86	> conditional helper
    87	> must carry the `**Unfaithful:**` docstring marker described in `AGENTS.md`.
    88	> Review such PRs against statement faithfulness and the documented discharge
    89	> plan, not merely against the temporary `sorry` count.
    90	
    91	### Axiom policy
    92	
    93	When an external mathematical result must remain unformalized temporarily,
    94	prefer a caller-supplied `Prop` hypothesis over a global `axiom`
    95	declaration, and add a regression check (for example a
    96	`Lean.collectAxioms`-based assertion, as in
    97	`MIPStarRE.LDT.Test.AxiomAudit`) so later refactors cannot silently widen
    98	the axiomatic base.
    99	
   100	This preference does not license proposition inputs on source-labelled paper
   101	theorems.  If the cited paper theorem does not assume the proposition, a
   102	caller-supplied `Prop` hypothesis is an additional theorem hypothesis, not a
   103	proof of the paper statement.  Use such hypotheses only for explicitly
   104	conditional auxiliary results, and keep the source-labelled theorem statement
   105	faithful to the paper.
   106	
   107	### Scaffolding that blocks real formalization
   108	
   109	This is a subtle but critical failure mode: **scaffolding definitions or
   110	theorem statements that do not faithfully represent the actual mathematics**,
   111	making them impossible to connect to real Mathlib-based proofs.
   112	
   113	Signs to watch for:
   114	
   115	- Custom type definitions for objects that already exist in Mathlib (e.g.,
   116	  defining a custom `Measurement` type instead of using Mathlib's
   117	  `MeasureTheory` or operator algebra API)
   118	- Theorem statements whose hypotheses or conclusions use project-local types
   119	  that are not definitionally equal to or coercible from the Mathlib versions
   120	- Scaffolded definitions that compile but encode the wrong mathematical
   121	  semantics (e.g., a "projective measurement" definition that does not enforce
   122	  the correct positivity or completeness conditions)
   123	- Intermediate lemmas stated in terms of scaffolding types that cannot be
   124	  connected upstream to Mathlib's API without reproving everything
   125	- Definitions that "work" for `sorry`-based proofs but fail when you try to
   126	  fill in real proofs using Mathlib lemmas (type mismatches, missing instances,
   127	  incompatible universes)
   128	
   129	When reviewing scaffolded code, ask: **Can a real proof be built on top of
   130	this?** If the types, instances, and API surface don't align with Mathlib, the
   131	scaffolding is actively harmful — it creates technical debt that blocks
   132	progress rather than enabling it.
   133	
   134	### Paper-labelled theorem statement drift
   135	
   136	A theorem advertised as the Lean formalization of a paper theorem is a blocker
   137	if its public statement has drifted from the cited paper statement.
   138	Changing a theorem away from the statement in `references/ldt-paper/` is
   139	strongly discouraged unless it is forced by faithful formal encoding or by a
   140	documented mathematical necessity.
   141	
   142	The most common failure mode is replacing an unformalized proof step by an
   143	extra hypothesis on the theorem itself.  This produces a true conditional
   144	theorem, but it is not the theorem stated in the paper.  In particular, do not
   145	repair a theorem such as `mainFormal` by adding assumptions named
   146	`BridgeHypotheses`, `Input`, `Residual`, `Package`, `RepairInput`, `Producer`,
   147	generic `Hypotheses` or `Assumptions` bundles, or similar, unless those
   148	assumptions are explicitly present in the cited paper statement.
   149	
   150	Conditional helpers are a last-resort quarantine for proof work that cannot yet
   151	be closed.  Before introducing one, state the missing intermediate fact as a
   152	named lemma or theorem to be proved from the paper hypotheses.  A conditional
   153	helper is permitted only when it has a paper-gap note or tracking issue, a named
   154	obligation-discharger target, and an explicit removal plan.  Its name must show
   155	that it is conditional, for example with `_of_...`, `_assuming_...`, or
   156	`conditional...`.  It must not be the declaration used by a source-labelled
   157	blueprint theorem with `\leanok`.
   158	
   159	Existing bridge hypotheses should be treated as proof debt.  Mine their proofs
   160	for reusable arguments, but do not keep a paper-labelled theorem in a
   161	strengthened form merely because the conditional version compiles.  If the
   162	bridge data cannot be derived from the paper hypotheses, the correct repair is
   163	to restore the paper-aligned theorem statement and leave the missing proof as a
   164	tracked `sorry`, rather than to keep the extra assumption on the theorem.
   165	
   166	Not every explicit Lean hypothesis is statement drift.  Side conditions needed
   167	to encode the paper's domain, such as nonemptiness, decidability, field-model
   168	instances, positivity of parameters, or denominator nonvanishing, may be
   169	faithful when the paper uses the corresponding objects without comment.  These
   170	conditions should still be reviewed.  The issue is whether the hypothesis is
   171	mathematical domain data implicit in the source, or an unproved intermediate
   172	step of the source proof.
   173	
   174	For every paper-labelled theorem change, require a statement integrity audit:
   175	
   176	- paper assumptions versus Lean assumptions;
   177	- paper conclusion versus Lean conclusion;
   178	- verdict: exact, faithful boundary hypotheses, extra assumptions, weakened
   179	  conclusion, or strengthened conclusion.
   180	
   181	### Source-statement proof gaps
   182	
   183	**For source-statement proof gaps**: Read
   184	[`paper-gaps/proof-gap-protocol.tex`](paper-gaps/proof-gap-protocol.tex) when a
   185	proof is blocked by a bridge, residual, repair, input, package, or obligation
   186	structure.  It explains when to introduce an internal obligation theorem, why
   187	conditional helpers are exceptional temporary quarantine objects, and why a
   188	tracked `sorry` is preferable to a strengthened source theorem statement.

    11	\author{}

    15	\maketitle
    16	
    17	\section{Purpose}
    18	
    19	When a formalization relies on a cited mathematical source, the cited source
    20	should remain intact.  It is a source, not an errata file.  If a possible gap,
    21	missing hypothesis, incorrect numerical constant, or other mathematical
    22	discrepancy is found, the matter should be recorded in a separate LaTeX note.
    23	In this repository such notes live under \path{docs/paper-gaps/}.  The same
    24	principle applies when the formal development has already diverged from the
    25	cited source, for instance by changing a statement so that it compiles, or by
    26	using a different mathematical route because an available formal-library theorem
    27	has a slightly different form.  Such a note is a mathematical note first, and a
    28	record of the formalization second: it should be readable by a mathematician or
    29	mathematical physicist who has not followed the issue discussion.
    30	
    31	The note should isolate the mathematical mechanism.  It should say what the
    32	cited source asserts, what the cited results actually imply, where a term or
    33	hypothesis is lost, and what statement the formal development proves instead.
    34	If the formal proof takes a different route, the note should explain the
    35	replacement argument and the hypotheses on which it rests.  This is especially
    36	important when the proof uses a theorem, construction, or convention from
    37	Mathlib which is not part of the cited argument.  In that case the note should
    38	state the Mathlib result in ordinary mathematical language, explain how it is
    39	specialized to the notation of the paper, and compare its hypotheses and
    40	conclusion with the step it replaces.  It should not merely say that \Lean{} did
    41	not accept a proof, that the modified proof compiles, or that a named library
    42	lemma was applied.
    43	
    44	The documents in this directory should themselves follow this standard.  A
    45	policy or template which reads like a checklist will tend to produce checklist
    46	notes; the examples and templates should therefore be written as mathematical
    47	prose.
    48	
    49	\section{Concision and Readability}
    50	
    51	A paper-gap note should be short enough that a reader can understand the issue
    52	in one sitting.  The first page should answer four questions: what the source
    53	uses, how hard the remaining formal work is, what the formalization or audit
    54	checked, and what the current verdict is.  Begin with a short
    55	\emph{At a glance} section when the note concerns an open or recently resolved
    56	formalization task.  That section should estimate the difficulty, the rough
    57	implementation weight, the split between Mathlib reuse and project-local work,
    58	and the key Mathlib APIs or modules.  Use honest ranges, not false precision.
    59	
    60	The \emph{Key theorem forms} section should be Section~2, immediately after
    61	\emph{At a glance}.  Put the theorem forms before the source details so the
    62	reader knows what the formalization is aiming to prove.  After that, keep the
    63	source assertion, the mechanism being checked, the blueprint/formal comparison,
    64	and the conclusion.  Use more sections only when a counterexample or long
    65	derivation genuinely needs room.
    66	
    67	Keep background to the minimum needed for the local point.  Prefer one clear
    68	special case over a general restatement of the surrounding theorem.  Use displayed
    69	equations for the source assertion, the key calculation, and the theorem forms;
    70	avoid displays for traceability data, declaration names, or long lists.  The
    71	blueprint/formal comparison should be compact and should not repeat the theorem
    72	forms.  The section ``Form of the Note'' below specifies where traceability data
    73	belongs; the body should read as mathematical prose, not as a log.
    74	
    75	If the verdict is that there is no mathematical discrepancy, say so plainly and
    76	stop.  Keep the conclusion highly compact, normally under twenty source lines.
    77	If the only remaining work is an implementation task, name it briefly and link
    78	the issue or pull request in a footnote.
    79	
    80	\section{When the Investigation Starts}
    81	
    82	The investigation starts when the obstruction appears to be mathematical rather
    83	than merely formal.  No final judgement is needed at this stage.  It is enough
    84	that, after reading the relevant source and attempting the corresponding formal
    85	statement, the proof seems to require a different scalar, an additional
    86	hypothesis, a different tensor placement, a distinction between two objects which
    87	the prose identifies, or an auxiliary assertion not supplied by the cited
    88	argument.
    89	
    90	The same investigation should also start when such a deviation is discovered
    91	after the fact.  If the existing formal development or informal blueprint has
    92	already changed the statement, strengthened a hypothesis, weakened a conclusion,
    93	inserted an unadvertised lemma, or replaced the cited proof by a different
    94	formal-library argument, the mathematical change should be documented even if all
    95	relevant files already compile.
    96	
    97	At this early stage the purpose is to preserve the question while it is still
    98	local.  The note may later conclude that the matter is only notational, that an
    99	intermediate estimate in the cited source needs a harmless correction, that a
   100	missing hypothesis is genuinely needed, or that no discrepancy remains.  Thus
   101	the trigger is not the severity of the eventual verdict, but the appearance of a
   102	real mismatch between the cited reasoning and the statement that can be
   103	formalized.
   104	
   105	A failed tactic search, a missing formal lemma, or an inconvenient coercion is
   106	not enough.  The obstruction must survive translation back into ordinary
   107	mathematics.
   108	
   109	Sometimes an investigation uncovers an improvement that is not a discrepancy:
   110	the formalization works correctly, but it could be simplified by using an
   111	existing library, replacing a custom type, or adopting a cleaner proof route.
   112	These are not, by themselves, paper-gap notes.  They are action items.  When
   113	such an improvement is identified, open a GitHub issue or pull request that
   114	describes the proposed change.  If the investigation also produces a paper-gap
   115	note, link the issue or pull request from that note: the note records the
   116	mathematical justification, and the issue or pull request drives the
   117	implementation.
   118	
   119	\section{When to Write a Note}
   120	
   121	A note should be written once the source argument and the formal proof no longer
   122	match as mathematical arguments.  This includes, for instance, a numerical
   123	estimate whose constant does not follow from the cited lemma, a displayed
   124	conclusion which uses an unstated hypothesis, or a step in which two objects are
   125	identified although they must remain distinct.  In analytic, algebraic,
   126	probabilistic, or quantum arguments, such distinctions may concern the domain of
   127	a map, the placement of a tensor factor, the type of an outcome, the distinction
   128	between a structure and a substructure, or the scalar carried by an approximation
   129	relation.
   130	
   131	A note is required when an audit finds that a Lean declaration associated with a
   132	source-labelled statement has acquired an extra non-source hypothesis, such as
   133	bridge, residual, repair, producer, or obligation-structure data.  Such a
   134	declaration is temporary proof debt, not a replacement for the source theorem,
   135	and should not be introduced merely to avoid a \verb|sorry|.  The note must say
   136	plainly that the Lean result is conditional, identify the source-faithful theorem
   137	form that remains to be proved, and give the intended obligation discharger or
   138	removal plan.  The blueprint should not mark the source-labelled statement with
   139	\verb|\leanok| by pointing to this conditional helper.
   140	
   141	Changing a Lean theorem away from the statement in
   142	\path{references/ldt-paper/} is strongly discouraged.  A paper-gap note should
   143	not make such a change look routine: it should explain the mathematical
   144	necessity, or else classify the change as proof debt to be removed.
   145	
   146	When an existing conditional helper is audited, the first task is to extract any
   147	argument it already contains into source-faithful lemmas.  If the remaining
   148	bridge hypothesis cannot be derived from the paper hypotheses, the formal
   149	development should restore the source theorem statement and record the missing
   150	proof obligation explicitly, rather than retaining the strengthened statement as
   151	though it were the paper theorem.
   152	
   153	This requirement is not meant to classify every explicit Lean side condition as
   154	a discrepancy.  Positivity, nonemptiness, decidability, field-model instances,
   155	and denominator nonvanishing hypotheses may be faithful encodings of the domain
   156	in which the paper's theorem is stated.  The note should distinguish such
   157	boundary hypotheses from hypotheses that supply an unproved step of the paper
   158	argument.
   159	
   160	A note is also appropriate when the proof becomes formal only after changing an
   161	intermediate scalar, weakening a conclusion, strengthening a hypothesis, or
   162	inserting an additional lemma which is not simply an expansion of the cited
   163	argument.  These are mathematical changes, even when they are harmless for the
   164	final theorem.  It is likewise appropriate when an available formal-library
   165	theorem proves the needed result under a somewhat different formulation from the
   166	cited source.  In that case the note should be deliberately pedagogical.  It
   167	should explain, in ordinary mathematical language, what the replacement result
   168	says, how it is specialized, which hypotheses are new or differently packaged,
   169	and why the resulting statement is a legitimate substitute for the step in the
   170	cited argument.  If the issue remains open after reasonable attempts, the note
   171	should say what has been checked and what remains unknown.
   172	
   173	\section{Counterexamples}
   174	
   175	If the cited assertion appears to be false, the note should not stop at saying
   176	that the proof cannot be formalized.  It should give the counterexample, or the
   177	smallest relevant part of it, in ordinary mathematical notation.  The example
   178	should be accompanied by enough verification that the reader can see both sides:
   179	the hypotheses of the cited assertion hold, and its conclusion fails.
   180	
   181	When feasible, the counterexample should also be formalized in \Lean{}.  This is
   182	especially valuable when the example is finite, algebraic, computational, or
   183	otherwise small enough that the failure can be checked without reproducing the
   184	whole surrounding theory.  The note should then state the mathematical content
   185	of the checked counterexample and identify the corresponding Lean declaration in
   186	a footnote.  The Lean file is not a substitute for the prose: the prose should
   187	still explain why the example refutes the cited assertion.
   188	
   189	\section{Revision of a Note}
   190	
   191	A paper-gap note may be provisional.  It may begin as soon as the mathematical
   192	obstruction has been isolated well enough to state the question, and it may be
   193	revised as the calculation, the blueprint, or the corresponding \Lean{}
   194	declarations become clearer.  The first version need not know the final
   195	classification, but it should say plainly which mathematical point is known and
   196	which point remains unsettled.
   197	
   198	Later revisions should not make the note into a chronological log.  They should
   199	rewrite the document so that it remains a coherent account of the present
   200	mathematical understanding.  If the verdict changes, the conclusion should state
   201	the current verdict; the linked issue or pull request can preserve the earlier
   202	discussion.
   203	
   204	\section{Form of the Note}
   205	
   206	Each note should stand on its own.  It should give the date, cite the relevant
   207	source article, and provide enough traceability for the reader to locate the
   208	original passage and the project discussion.  GitHub issues and pull requests may
   209	be linked with \verb|\href|, and source files, line ranges, and labels should be
   210	recorded when they help the reader check the claim.  These references should
   211	serve the exposition rather than govern it: the main text should be organized
   212	around the mathematical assertion and its proof.
   213	
   214	The note should introduce its notation before using it.  Symbols for
   215	measurements, tensor factors, approximation relations, and error parameters
   216	should be named in prose.  If an approximation relation is state-dependent, the
   217	state should be named, or its defining expression should be given when this can
   218	be done briefly.  Only after the notation is in place should the note state the
   219	assertion in the cited source, using a bibliographic citation such as
   220	\verb|\cite[Section~...]{...}| when the section or chapter is known.
   221	
   222	Only the relevant hypotheses should be reproduced.  If the question is a scalar
   223	substitution, a missing term, or a missing hypothesis, the note should not quote
   224	a long unrelated part of the proof.  It should give the cited lemma or
   225	proposition in the special case actually used, then display the calculation or
   226	logical implication in which the discrepancy appears.
   227	
   228	Displayed equations should be used with restraint.  They are appropriate for the
   229	source estimate being checked, the cited estimate in the form actually used, and
   230	the calculation where a term or hypothesis appears or disappears.  When a
   231	displayed equation is identified by a source label, the label should appear on
   232	the right of the display, while the surrounding prose refers to the mathematical
   233	assertion itself.  The standard \texttt{amsmath} command \verb|\tag| is the
   234	right mechanism for this; a separate local convention should be introduced only
   235	if the standard mechanism is genuinely insufficient.  For a multi-line aligned
   236	display, tag the individual lines that carry the source information rather than
   237	forcing a long combined label below the equations.  Short
   238	scalar definitions and elementary inequalities should remain inline when the
   239	sentence reads better that way.  As in ordinary mathematical writing, a displayed
   240	formula is part of the surrounding sentence and should be punctuated accordingly.

1	import MIPStarRE.QPBT.Algebra.PauliTheorems
     2	import MIPStarRE.QPBT.Observables.Defs
     3	
     4	/-!
     5	# Expanded registers and point measurements
     6	
     7	This module adjoins two EPR pairs to a heterogeneous Pauli-basis-test strategy,
     8	records the four register placements used in the analysis, and defines the
     9	expanded point observables and measurements.
    10	
    11	## References
    12	
    13	The constructions formalize `def:expanded-state`, `def:expanded-observables`,
    14	`def:expanded-point-measurement`, and `def:expanded-point-trace-projection` in
    15	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch14_qpbt_observables.tex:760-874`. Their paper source is
    16	`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:367-418`.
    17	-/
    18	
    19	open scoped BigOperators Matrix MatrixOrder ComplexOrder
    20	
    21	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    22	
    23	open MIPStarRE.LDT MIPStarRE.Quantum
    24	
    25	noncomputable section
    26	
    27	/-- The six registers `AA'A''BB'B''`, retaining distinct Alice and Bob local
    28	spaces. This is the register index type of `def:expanded-state`, paper
    29	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:367-372`, blueprint
    30	`ch14_qpbt_observables.tex:760-781`. -/
    31	abbrev SixReg (P : AdmissibleParams) (ιA ιB : Type*) :=
    32	  (ιA × (PauliRegister P × PauliRegister P)) ×
    33	    (ιB × (PauliRegister P × PauliRegister P))
    34	
    35	/-- Equality of six-register indices is supplied by classical decidability for
    36	the register type. This is the index set of `def:expanded-state`; blueprint
    37	`ch14_qpbt_observables.tex:760-781`. -/
    38	noncomputable instance sixRegDecidableEq (P : AdmissibleParams)
    39	    (ιA ιB : Type*) : DecidableEq (SixReg P ιA ιB) :=
    40	  Classical.decEq _
    41	
    42	/-- Reassociate the tensor product of the strategy state and two EPR states
    43	directly into register order `AA'A''BB'B''` for
    44	`eq:def-psihat`, paper `14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:367-372`. -/
    45	def sixRegShuffle (P : AdmissibleParams) (ιA ιB : Type*) :
    46	    (((ιA × ιB) × (PauliRegister P × PauliRegister P)) ×
    47	        (PauliRegister P × PauliRegister P)) ≃ SixReg P ιA ιB where
    48	  toFun p := ((p.1.1.1, (p.1.2.1, p.1.2.2)),
    49	    (p.1.1.2, (p.2.1, p.2.2)))
    50	  invFun p := (((p.1.1, p.2.1), (p.1.2.1, p.1.2.2)),
    51	    (p.2.2.1, p.2.2.2))
    52	  left_inv p := by cases p; rfl
    53	  right_inv p := by cases p; rfl
    54	
    55	/-- The four placements `AA'`, `BA''`, `BB'`, and `AB''` used explicitly in
    56	the chapter-14 consistency statements. Paper
    57	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:420-450`; blueprint
    58	`ch14_qpbt_observables.tex:876-922`. -/
    59	inductive Placement where
    60	  | AA'
    61	  | BA''
    62	  | BB'
    63	  | AB''
    64	  deriving DecidableEq, Repr, Inhabited, Fintype
    65	
    66	/-- The strategy-player side supplying the local Hilbert space in each of the
    67	four register placements at paper
    68	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:420-450`. -/
    69	def Placement.side : Placement → PlayerSide
    70	  | .AA' => .alice
    71	  | .BA'' => .bob
    72	  | .BB' => .bob
    73	  | .AB'' => .alice
    74	
    75	namespace ProjectiveSetting
    76	
    77	variable {P : AdmissibleParams} {ε : ℝ}
    78	
    79	/-- A strategy-local register paired with one generalized-Pauli register. This
    80	is the operator space in `def:expanded-observables`, paper
    81	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:374-382`. -/
    82	abbrev ExpandedLocalSpace (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε) (side : PlayerSide) :=
    83	  S.LocalSpace side × PauliRegister P
    84	
    85	/-- The strategy state tensored with EPR states on `A'A''` and `B'B''`, in the
    86	six-register order. This is `eq:def-psihat`, paper
    87	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:367-372`, blueprint
    88	`ch14_qpbt_observables.tex:760-781`. -/
    89	noncomputable def psiHat (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε) :
    90	    EuclideanSpace ℂ (SixReg P S.toStrategy.ιA S.toStrategy.ιB) := by
    91	  classical
    92	  exact
    93	    reindexState (sixRegShuffle P S.toStrategy.ιA S.toStrategy.ιB)
    94	      (vecTensor
    95	        (vecTensor S.toStrategy.ψ (eprState (PauliRegister P)))
    96	        (eprState (PauliRegister P)))
    97	
    98	/-- Place an operator on one of `AA'`, `BA''`, `BB'`, or `AB''`, with the
    99	identity on all remaining registers. The input local space is determined by
   100	the placement, so no equality between the player spaces is assumed. Paper
   101	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:420-450`; blueprint
   102	`ch14_qpbt_observables.tex:876-922`. -/
   103	noncomputable def place (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε) (p : Placement)
   104	    (O : Op (S.ExpandedLocalSpace p.side)) :
   105	    Op (SixReg P S.toStrategy.ιA S.toStrategy.ιB) :=
   106	  fun i j =>
   107	    match p with
   108	    | .AA' =>
   109	        O (i.1.1, i.1.2.1) (j.1.1, j.1.2.1) *
   110	          (1 : Op (PauliRegister P)) i.1.2.2 j.1.2.2 *
   111	          (1 : Op S.toStrategy.ιB) i.2.1 j.2.1 *
   112	          (1 : Op (PauliRegister P)) i.2.2.1 j.2.2.1 *
   113	          (1 : Op (PauliRegister P)) i.2.2.2 j.2.2.2
   114	    | .BA'' =>
   115	        (1 : Op S.toStrategy.ιA) i.1.1 j.1.1 *
   116	          (1 : Op (PauliRegister P)) i.1.2.1 j.1.2.1 *
   117	          O (i.2.1, i.1.2.2) (j.2.1, j.1.2.2) *
   118	          (1 : Op (PauliRegister P)) i.2.2.1 j.2.2.1 *
   119	          (1 : Op (PauliRegister P)) i.2.2.2 j.2.2.2
   120	    | .BB' =>
   121	        (1 : Op S.toStrategy.ιA) i.1.1 j.1.1 *
   122	          (1 : Op (PauliRegister P)) i.1.2.1 j.1.2.1 *
   123	          (1 : Op (PauliRegister P)) i.1.2.2 j.1.2.2 *
   124	          O (i.2.1, i.2.2.1) (j.2.1, j.2.2.1) *
   125	          (1 : Op (PauliRegister P)) i.2.2.2 j.2.2.2
   126	    | .AB'' =>
   127	        O (i.1.1, i.2.2.2) (j.1.1, j.2.2.2) *
   128	          (1 : Op (PauliRegister P)) i.1.2.1 j.1.2.1 *
   129	          (1 : Op (PauliRegister P)) i.1.2.2 j.1.2.2 *
   130	          (1 : Op S.toStrategy.ιB) i.2.1 j.2.1 *
   131	          (1 : Op (PauliRegister P)) i.2.2.1 j.2.2.1
   132	
   133	/-- The expanded observable
   134	`W^r(u) tensor tau^W(r * ind_m(u))` on a selected player side. This is
   135	Equation `eq:lc-23`, paper `14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:374-382`,
   136	blueprint `ch14_qpbt_observables.tex:783-807`. -/
   137	noncomputable def expObs (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε) (side : PlayerSide)
   138	    (W : PauliKind) (r : PauliScalar P) (u : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P) :
   139	    Op (S.ExpandedLocalSpace side) :=
   140	  heteroKron (S.pointObs side W r u)
   141	    (tauObservable W (fun h => r * indicatorVec u h))
   142	
   143	/-- The Fourier average defining the expanded point effect. This is the first
   144	display of `def:expanded-point-measurement`, paper
   145	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:384-418`, blueprint
   146	`ch14_qpbt_observables.tex:809-844`. -/
   147	noncomputable def expPointOp (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε) (side : PlayerSide)
   148	    (W : PauliKind) (u : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P) (a : PauliScalar P) :
   149	    Op (S.ExpandedLocalSpace side) :=
   150	  averageOperatorOverDistribution (uniformDistribution (PauliScalar P)) fun r =>
   151	    phaseSign (fixedBinTrace P.model (a * r)) • S.expObs side W r u
   152	
   153	/-- The Pauli-register projector onto labels whose low-degree encoding has
   154	value `a` at `u`. This is Equation `eq:qld-point-obs-def`, paper
   155	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:389-394`, blueprint
   156	`ch14_qpbt_observables.tex:809-844`. -/
   157	noncomputable def tauPointProj (W : PauliKind)
   158	    (u : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P) (a : PauliScalar P) : Op (PauliRegister P) :=
   159	  ∑ h ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun h : PauliRegister P =>
   160	      dotProduct h (indicatorVec u) = a),
   161	    pauliProj W h
   162	
   163	/-- Expanded point effects are positive semidefinite. This is the positivity
   164	obligation in `def:expanded-point-measurement`, paper
   165	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:384-418`. -/
   166	theorem expPointOp_nonneg (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε) (side : PlayerSide)
   167	    (W : PauliKind) (u : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P) (a : PauliScalar P) :
   168	    0 ≤ S.expPointOp side W u a := by
   169	  sorry
   170	
   171	/-- Expanded point effects sum to the identity. This is the completeness
   172	obligation in `def:expanded-point-measurement`, paper
   173	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:384-418`. -/

    31	/-! ## The canonical scalar identification -/
    32	
    33	/-- Identify the direct extended game's scalar field with the Pauli scalar
    34	field.  Both are selected by `fixedFieldModel`; only their proof argument for
    35	admissibility differs. -/
    36	noncomputable def extendedDirectScalarEquiv (P : AdmissibleParams) :
    37	    DirectScalarQ P.extendedDirectLd ≃+* PauliScalar P := by
    38	  have h : P.extendedDirectLd.hq = P.hq := Subsingleton.elim _ _
    39	  cases h
    40	  exact RingEquiv.refl _
    41	
    42	/-- Transport an extended direct point into the canonical Pauli scalar field. -/
    43	def directPointToPauli (P : AdmissibleParams)
    44	    (u : Fin P.extendedDirectLd.m -> DirectScalarQ P.extendedDirectLd) :
    45	    Fin (2 * P.m + 2) -> PauliScalar P :=
    46	  fun i => extendedDirectScalarEquiv P (u i)

    48	/-! ## Finite direct-line carrier -/
    49	
    50	/-- A finite code for directly indexed lines, omitting only proof fields. -/
    51	private abbrev DirectLineDescCode (D : DirectLdParams) :=
    52	  ((Fin D.m -> DirectScalarQ D) × Fin D.m) ⊕
    53	    ((Fin D.m -> DirectScalarQ D) × Fin D.m ×
    54	      (Fin D.m -> DirectScalarQ D))
    55	
    56	/-- Encode a directly indexed line by its tag and mathematical data. -/
    57	private def directLineDescCode (D : DirectLdParams) :
    58	    DirectLineDesc D -> DirectLineDescCode D
    59	  | .axis base index _ => .inl (base, index)
    60	  | .diagonal base index direction _ _ => .inr (base, index, direction)
    61	
    62	/-- The direct-line code is injective by proof irrelevance. -/
    63	private theorem directLineDescCode_injective (D : DirectLdParams) :
    64	    Function.Injective (directLineDescCode D) := by
    65	  intro line line' h
    66	  cases line with
    67	  | axis base index baseFixed =>
    68	      cases line' with
    69	      | axis base' index' baseFixed' =>
    70	          simp only [directLineDescCode, Sum.inl.injEq, Prod.mk.injEq] at h
    71	          rcases h with ⟨rfl, rfl⟩
    72	          rfl
    73	      | diagonal => simp [directLineDescCode] at h
    74	  | diagonal base index direction baseFixed prefixZero =>
    75	      cases line' with
    76	      | axis => simp [directLineDescCode] at h
    77	      | diagonal base' index' direction' baseFixed' prefixZero' =>
    78	          simp only [directLineDescCode, Sum.inr.injEq, Prod.mk.injEq] at h
    79	          rcases h with ⟨rfl, rfl, rfl⟩
    80	          rfl
    81	
    82	/-- Directly indexed line descriptions form a finite type. -/
    83	noncomputable instance directLineDescFintype (D : DirectLdParams) :
    84	    Fintype (DirectLineDesc D) :=
    85	  Fintype.ofInjective (directLineDescCode D) (directLineDescCode_injective D)

    87	/-! ## Combined point and line measurements -/
    88	
    89	/-- Projective joint point measurements and their ordered consistency
    90	guarantees from `lem:qld-4-10`, paper lines 689--709.  The `XZ` and `ZX`
    91	products are retained as distinct fields. -/
    92	structure CombinedPointsWitness {P : AdmissibleParams} {ε : ℝ}
    93	    (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε) (δ : ℝ) where
    94	  /-- The complete joint measurement on each player's expanded local space. -/
    95	  Q : (side : PlayerSide) ->
    96	    (Fin P.m -> PauliScalar P) ->
    97	    (Fin P.m -> PauliScalar P) ->
    98	    Measurement (PauliScalar P × PauliScalar P) (S.ExpandedLocalSpace side)
    99	  /-- Every joint point measurement is projective. -/
   100	  projective : ∀ side x z, Measurement.IsProjective (Q side x z)
   101	  /-- Joint point measurements agree across every directed opposite placement. -/
   102	  self_consistent : ∀ p1 p2 : Placement, p1.IsOpposite p2 ->
   103	    opFamilyDistSq
   104	      (uniformDistribution
   105	        ((Fin P.m -> PauliScalar P) × (Fin P.m -> PauliScalar P)))
   106	      (fun xz ab => S.place p1 ((Q p1.side xz.1 xz.2).effect ab))
   107	      (fun xz ab => S.place p2 ((Q p2.side xz.1 xz.2).effect ab))
   108	      S.psiHat <= δ
   109	  /-- Joint point measurements are close to the ordered `X`-then-`Z` product. -/
   110	  consistent_XZ : ∀ p1 p2 : Placement, p1.IsOpposite p2 ->
   111	    opFamilyDistSq
   112	      (uniformDistribution
   113	        ((Fin P.m -> PauliScalar P) × (Fin P.m -> PauliScalar P)))
   114	      (fun xz ab => S.place p1 ((Q p1.side xz.1 xz.2).effect ab))
   115	      (fun xz ab => S.place p2
   116	        ((S.pointMeasExp p2.side .X xz.1).effect ab.1 *
   117	          (S.pointMeasExp p2.side .Z xz.2).effect ab.2))
   118	      S.psiHat <= δ
   119	  /-- Joint point measurements are close to the ordered `Z`-then-`X` product. -/
   120	  consistent_ZX : ∀ p1 p2 : Placement, p1.IsOpposite p2 ->
   121	    opFamilyDistSq
   122	      (uniformDistribution
   123	        ((Fin P.m -> PauliScalar P) × (Fin P.m -> PauliScalar P)))
   124	      (fun xz ab => S.place p1 ((Q p1.side xz.1 xz.2).effect ab))
   125	      (fun xz ab => S.place p2
   126	        ((S.pointMeasExp p2.side .Z xz.2).effect ab.2 *
   127	          (S.pointMeasExp p2.side .X xz.1).effect ab.1))
   128	      S.psiHat <= δ
   129	
   130	/-- Joint line measurements and their evaluation consistency from
   131	`lem:qld-xz-lines`, paper lines 882--894.  Evaluation uses explicit `Option`
   132	outcomes, including the class of answers not determined at the sampled point. -/
   133	structure CombinedLinesWitness {P : AdmissibleParams} {ε δQ : ℝ}
   134	    (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε) (points : CombinedPointsWitness S δQ)
   135	    (δ : ℝ) where
   136	  /-- The complete paired-line measurement on each expanded local space. -/
   137	  T : (side : PlayerSide) ->
   138	    LineDesc P.toLdParams -> LineDesc P.toLdParams ->
   139	    Measurement
   140	      (DegPoly P.toLdParams (P.m * P.d) ×
   141	        DegPoly P.toLdParams (P.m * P.d))
   142	      (S.ExpandedLocalSpace side)
   143	  /-- On an axis-parallel X line, outcomes outside degree `d` have zero effect. -/
   144	  axis_degree_X : ∀ side lineX lineZ fX fZ,
   145	    lineX.kind = .axis -> Not (DegPoly.FitsDegree P.d fX) ->
   146	      (T side lineX lineZ).effect (fX, fZ) = 0
   147	  /-- On an axis-parallel Z line, outcomes outside degree `d` have zero effect. -/
   148	  axis_degree_Z : ∀ side lineX lineZ fX fZ,
   149	    lineZ.kind = .axis -> Not (DegPoly.FitsDegree P.d fZ) ->
   150	      (T side lineX lineZ).effect (fX, fZ) = 0
   151	  /-- Evaluated line pairs are consistent with the completed point-pair
   152	  measurement on every directed opposite placement. -/
   153	  consistent : ∀ p1 p2 : Placement, p1.IsOpposite p2 ->
   154	    consistencyDefect
   155	      (Distribution.prod (linePointDist P.toLdParams)
   156	        (linePointDist P.toLdParams))
   157	      (fun sample answer => S.place p1
   158	        (((T p1.side sample.1.1 sample.2.1).postprocess fun fs =>
   159	          (evalOpt sample.1.1 sample.1.2 fs.1,
   160	            evalOpt sample.2.1 sample.2.2 fs.2)).effect answer))
   161	      (fun sample answer => S.place p2
   162	        (((points.Q p2.side sample.1.2 sample.2.2).postprocess fun ab =>
   163	          (some ab.1, some ab.2)).effect answer))
   164	      S.psiHat <= δ

   166	/-! ## The subline distribution -/
   167	
   168	/-- A tuple consisting of an extended line and its projected X and Z lines. -/
   169	abbrev SubLineTriple (P : AdmissibleParams) :=
   170	  DirectLineDesc P.extendedDirectLd ×
   171	    (LineDesc P.toLdParams × LineDesc P.toLdParams)
   172	
   173	/-- An extended line tuple together with a point sampled uniformly on it. -/
   174	abbrev SubLinePointSample (P : AdmissibleParams) :=
   175	  SubLineTriple P ×
   176	    (Fin P.extendedDirectLd.m -> DirectScalarQ P.extendedDirectLd)
   177	
   178	/-- The shared restricted line kind and two coordinate indices in one mixture
   179	component of the subline law. -/
   180	abbrev SubLineComponent (P : AdmissibleParams) :=
   181	  LineKind × (Fin P.m × Fin P.m)
   182	
   183	/-- Select the restricted line-point distribution of a given kind and index. -/
   184	noncomputable def restrictedLinePointDist (P : AdmissibleParams)
   185	    (kind : LineKind) (i : Fin P.m) :
   186	    Distribution (LineDesc P.toLdParams × (Fin P.m -> PauliScalar P)) :=
   187	  match kind with
   188	  | .axis => restrictedALineDist P.toLdParams i
   189	  | .diagonal => restrictedDLineDist P.toLdParams i
   190	
   191	/-- Sample a subline tuple and then a uniform affine parameter on its
   192	extended line. -/
   193	noncomputable def subLinePointDist (P : AdmissibleParams)
   194	    (D : Distribution (SubLineTriple P)) :
   195	    Distribution (SubLinePointSample P) :=
   196	  (Distribution.prod D
   197	    (uniformDistribution (DirectScalarQ P.extendedDirectLd))).map fun sample =>
   198	      (sample.1, sample.1.1.base + sample.2 • sample.1.1.direction)
   199	
   200	/-- Retain the projected line pair and the X projection of an extended point. -/
   201	def subLineXProjection {P : AdmissibleParams} (sample : SubLinePointSample P) :
   202	    (LineDesc P.toLdParams × LineDesc P.toLdParams) ×
   203	      (Fin P.m -> PauliScalar P) :=
   204	  (sample.1.2, projX (directPointToPauli P sample.2))
   205	
   206	/-- Retain the projected line pair and the Z projection of an extended point. -/
   207	def subLineZProjection {P : AdmissibleParams} (sample : SubLinePointSample P) :
   208	    (LineDesc P.toLdParams × LineDesc P.toLdParams) ×
   209	      (Fin P.m -> PauliScalar P) :=
   210	  (sample.1.2, projZ (directPointToPauli P sample.2))
   211	
   212	/-- The X-point marginal associated with one restricted product component. -/
   213	noncomputable def subLineXComponentDist (P : AdmissibleParams)
   214	    (component : SubLineComponent P) :
   215	    Distribution
   216	      ((LineDesc P.toLdParams × LineDesc P.toLdParams) ×
   217	        (Fin P.m -> PauliScalar P)) :=
   218	  (Distribution.prod
   219	    (restrictedLinePointDist P component.1 component.2.1)
   220	    ((restrictedLinePointDist P component.1 component.2.2).map Prod.fst)).map
   221	      fun sample => ((sample.1.1, sample.2), sample.1.2)
   222	
   223	/-- The Z-point marginal associated with one restricted product component. -/
   224	noncomputable def subLineZComponentDist (P : AdmissibleParams)
   225	    (component : SubLineComponent P) :
   226	    Distribution
   227	      ((LineDesc P.toLdParams × LineDesc P.toLdParams) ×
   228	        (Fin P.m -> PauliScalar P)) :=
   229	  (Distribution.prod
   230	    ((restrictedLinePointDist P component.1 component.2.1).map Prod.fst)
   231	    (restrictedLinePointDist P component.1 component.2.2)).map
   232	      fun sample => ((sample.1, sample.2.1), sample.2.2)
   233	
   234	/-- The subline distribution of `lem:qld-sublines`, paper lines 1063--1069.
   235	Its source-mixture field records the X and Z point marginals separately; it
   236	does not assert a joint conditional law for the pair of projected points. -/
   237	structure SubLineWitness (P : AdmissibleParams) where
   238	  /-- The actual distribution of an extended line and two projected lines. -/
   239	  D : Distribution (SubLineTriple P)
   240	  /-- The distribution has total mass one. -/
   241	  isProbability : D.IsProbability
   242	  /-- Its extended-line marginal is the direct line-point marginal. -/
   243	  extended_marginal : D.map Prod.fst =
   244	    (directLinePointDist P.extendedDirectLd).map Prod.fst
   245	  /-- Every point of an extended line projects onto both stored source lines. -/
   246	  incidence : ∀ sample ∈ D.support, ∀ u ∈ sample.1.pointSet,
   247	    projX (directPointToPauli P u) ∈ sample.2.1.pointSet ∧
   248	      projZ (directPointToPauli P u) ∈ sample.2.2.pointSet
   249	  /-- Each line triple carries affine data sufficient for
   250	  `combineLinePoly_spec`. -/

     4	/-!
     5	# Polynomial combination and restricted line distributions
     6	
     7	This file contains the concrete definitions at the foundation of the
     8	Chapter 15 combining argument.  A pair of bounded individual-degree
     9	polynomials is embedded into the two coordinate blocks of an extended
    10	polynomial.  On lines, explicit affine reparameterizations are composed with
    11	coefficient-list polynomials.  The original-dimensional restricted line laws
    12	are formed before decoding, while their field seed is still present.
    13	
    14	## References
    15	
    16	The combining map is `def:combine-map` in
    17	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch15_qpbt_combining.tex:445-480`, with paper origin
    18	`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:970-989`.
    19	The restricted laws are `def:ith-restricted-line` in blueprint lines 578--592,
    20	with paper origin in the same source at lines 1038--1048.
    21	-/
    22	
    23	open scoped BigOperators
    24	
    25	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    26	
    27	open MIPStarRE.LDT
    28	open MIPStarRE.LDT.Preliminaries
    29	
    30	noncomputable section
    31	
    32	/-- The bounded individual-degree polynomial outcome used by the global
    33	pair measurement.  This is the actual `polyFunc` subtype from
    34	`def:polyfunc`, not a coefficient-box replacement. -/
    35	noncomputable abbrev Poly (P : AdmissibleParams) :=
    36	  ↥(MIPStarRE.LDT.Preliminaries.polyFunc P.m (PauliScalar P) P.d)
    37	
    38	/-- Pairs of bounded polynomial representatives returned by the global
    39	measurement in `lem:qld-4-7`. -/
    40	noncomputable abbrev PolyPair (P : AdmissibleParams) := Poly P × Poly P
    41	
    42	/-- Split the extended coordinate set into the `X` block, the `Z` block, and
    43	the two scalar coordinates.  This is formalization-only coordinate plumbing
    44	for `def:combine-map`, blueprint
    45	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch15_qpbt_combining.tex:445-480`, paper
    46	`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:970-989`. -/
    47	def finCombineEquiv (m : ℕ) :
    48	    Fin (2 * m + 2) ≃ ((Fin m ⊕ Fin m) ⊕ Fin 2) :=
    49	  (finCongr (by omega)).trans
    50	    (finSumFinEquiv.symm.trans
    51	      (Equiv.sumCongr finSumFinEquiv.symm (Equiv.refl (Fin 2))))
    52	
    53	/-- Embed an `X`-block coordinate into the extended coordinate set. -/
    54	def embX (m : ℕ) : Fin m → Fin (2 * m + 2) :=
    55	  fun i => (finCombineEquiv m).symm (.inl (.inl i))
    56	
    57	/-- Embed a `Z`-block coordinate into the extended coordinate set. -/
    58	def embZ (m : ℕ) : Fin m → Fin (2 * m + 2) :=
    59	  fun i => (finCombineEquiv m).symm (.inl (.inr i))
    60	
    61	/-- The extended coordinate occupied by the scalar `alpha`. -/
    62	def alphaVar (m : ℕ) : Fin (2 * m + 2) :=
    63	  (finCombineEquiv m).symm (.inr 0)
    64	
    65	/-- The extended coordinate occupied by the scalar `beta`. -/
    66	def betaVar (m : ℕ) : Fin (2 * m + 2) :=
    67	  (finCombineEquiv m).symm (.inr 1)
    68	
    69	/-- Project an extended point onto its `X` coordinate block. -/

     6	
     7	The definitions are the finite-dimensional forms of `def:consistency` and

    12	open scoped BigOperators
    13	
    14	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT

    17	
    18	/-- The off-diagonal defect in `def:consistency`, blueprint
    19	`ch12_qpbt_games.tex:195-208`, paper `06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:232-248`. -/
    20	noncomputable def consistencyDefect {X α ι : Type*}
    21	    [Fintype X] [DecidableEq X] [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α]
    22	    [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    23	    (μ : Distribution X) (A B : X → α → Op ι)
    24	    (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) : ℝ :=
    25	  avgOver μ (fun x =>
    26	    ∑ a : α, ∑ b : α,
    27	      if a = b then 0 else
    28	        (inner ℂ ψ ((EuclideanSpace.equiv ι ℂ).symm
    29	          ((A x a * B x b).mulVec ψ))).re)
    30	
    31	/-- The quantitative relation in `def:consistency`, blueprint
    32	`ch12_qpbt_games.tex:195-208`, paper `06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:232-248`. -/
    33	def IsConsistentWithin {X α ι : Type*}
    34	    [Fintype X] [DecidableEq X] [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α]
    35	    [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    36	    (μ : Distribution X) (A B : X → α → Op ι)
    37	    (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) (δ : ℝ) : Prop :=
    38	  consistencyDefect μ A B ψ ≤ δ
    39	
    40	/-- Unit-alphabet specialization of `def:povm-distance`, blueprint
    41	`ch12_qpbt_games.tex:219-226`, paper `06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:258-271`. -/
    42	noncomputable def opDistSq {X ι : Type*}
    43	    [Fintype X] [DecidableEq X] [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    44	    (μ : Distribution X) (M N : X → Op ι) (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) : ℝ :=
    45	  opFamilyDistSq μ (fun x (_ : Unit) => M x) (fun x (_ : Unit) => N x) ψ
    46	
    47	/-- The unit-alphabet operator distance equals its one-outcome family form from
    48	`def:povm-distance`, blueprint `ch12_qpbt_games.tex:219-226`, paper
    49	`06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:258-271`. -/
    50	theorem opDistSq_eq_opFamilyDistSq {X ι : Type*}
    51	    [Fintype X] [DecidableEq X] [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    52	    (μ : Distribution X) (M N : X → Op ι) (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) :
    53	    opDistSq μ M N ψ = opFamilyDistSq μ (fun x (_ : Unit) => M x)
    54	      (fun x (_ : Unit) => N x) ψ := rfl
    55	
    56	/-- The strategy-distance relation `def:strategy-distance`. The two strategies'
    57	local Hilbert spaces are identified, and both measurement distances are
    58	evaluated on the first strategy's state. Blueprint
    59	`ch12_qpbt_games.tex:228-237`, paper `06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:273-285`. -/
    60	structure AreCloseStrategies (G : Game) (S S' : Strategy G) (δ : ℝ) : Prop where
    61	  /-- Identification of Alice's local Hilbert spaces. -/
    62	  hA : S.ιA = S'.ιA
    63	  /-- Identification of Bob's local Hilbert spaces. -/
    64	  hB : S.ιB = S'.ιB
    65	  state : stateDistSq S.ψ (reindexState
    66	      (Equiv.prodCongr (Equiv.cast hA).symm (Equiv.cast hB).symm) S'.ψ) ≤ δ
    67	  alice : opFamilyDistSq (G.μ.map Prod.fst)
    68	      (fun x a => heteroKron ((S.A x).effect a) 1)
    69	      (fun x a => heteroKron (reindexOp (Equiv.cast hA) ((S'.A x).effect a)) 1)
    70	      S.ψ ≤ δ
    71	  bob : opFamilyDistSq (G.μ.map Prod.snd)
    72	      (fun y b => heteroKron 1 ((S.B y).effect b))
    73	      (fun y b => heteroKron 1 (reindexOp (Equiv.cast hB) ((S'.B y).effect b)))
    74	      S.ψ ≤ δ
    75	
    76	end MIPStarRE.QPBT

     3	/-!
     4	# Quantitative state and operator distances
     5	
     6	The blueprint uses asymptotic `approx` notation.  The skeleton records the
     7	corresponding squared norm functionals explicitly, leaving universal-constant
     8	estimates to later proof stages.
     9	
    10	## References
    11	
    12	These are `def:state-distance` and `def:povm-distance` in
    13	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:171-220`; the paper origin is
    14	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:219-271`.
    15	-/
    16	
    17	open scoped BigOperators
    18	
    19	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    20	
    21	open MIPStarRE.LDT
    22	open MIPStarRE.Quantum
    23	
    24	/--
    25	Squared Euclidean distance between pure states.  Blueprint `def:state-distance`
    26	(`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:171-179`), paper origin
    27	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:219-271`.
    28	-/
    29	noncomputable def stateDistSq {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι]
    30	    [DecidableEq ι]
    31	    (ψ φ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) : ℝ :=
    32	  ‖ψ - φ‖ ^ 2
    33	
    34	/--
    35	Average squared state-dependent distance between two operator families.  This
    36	is `def:povm-distance` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:203-210`,
    37	with paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:219-271`.
    38	-/
    39	noncomputable def opFamilyDistSq {X α ι : Type*}
    40	    [Fintype α] [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    41	    (μ : Distribution X) (M N : X → α → Op ι)
    42	    (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) : ℝ :=
    43	  avgOver μ (fun x =>
    44	    ∑ a : α, ‖applyOperatorToState (M x a - N x a) ψ‖ ^ 2)
    45	
    46	end MIPStarRE.QPBT

  1415	 \subsection{Pulling the $X$ and $Z$ measurements apart}
  1416	\label{sec:separating}
  1417	
  1418	
  1419	Recall the decoding map of the low-degree code defined in \Cref{sec:ld-encoding}. This map takes in a polynomial $g \in \ideg_{d,m}(\F_q)$ and returns a string $\coded(g) \in \F_q^{\nqubits}$ consisting of the evaluations of $g$ on the points in the hypercube $\{0,1\}^m$.
  1420	We now use this decoding map to construct a new set of measurement operators out of $\hat{S}$.
  1421	First, we introduce some notation. For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$ and all degree $d$ polynomials $g: \F_q^m \to \F_q$ define projectors
  1422	\[ \hat{S}^X_g = \sum_{g_\zpt} \hat{S}_{g,g_\zpt} \quad  \text{and}  \quad \hat{S}^Z_g = \sum_{g_\xpt} \hat{S}_{g_\xpt,g}\;,\]
  1423	where the measurement $\{\hat{S}_{g_\xpt,g_\zpt} \}$  is given by \Cref{lem:qld-4-7}.
  1424	
  1425	For all $W \in \{X, Z\}$, $\tilde{u} \in \F_q^{\nqubits}$, and $a \in \F_q$, define the projector
  1426	\begin{equation}\label{eq:def-tauwu}
  1427	 \tau^{W}_{a}(\tilde{u}) = \sum_{h \in \F_q^{\nqubits} \,:\, h \cdot \tilde{u} = a} \tau^W_{h}
  1428	\end{equation}
  1429	where recall that $\tau^W_h$ is the projector corresponding to measuring $(\C^q)^{\otimes \nqubits}$ in the $W$ basis and obtaining $h \in \F_q^\nqubits$ as the outcome. For all $\tilde{u} \in \F_q^\nqubits$ define the projective measurement $\{ \tilde{M}^{W,\tilde{u}}_a \}_{a \in \F_q}$ by 
  1430		\begin{equation}
  1431		\label{eq:tilde_M}
  1432		\tilde{M}^{W,\tilde{u}}_a =  \sum_{g} \hat{S}^W_g \otimes \tau_{(\coded(g) \cdot \tilde{u}) - a}^W(\tilde{u})\;.
  1433		\end{equation}
  1434		If $\hat{S}^W_g$ is viewed as an operator acting on registers $\alice \alice'$ (resp. $\bob \bob'$) then we view $\tilde{M}^{W,\tilde{u}}_a$ as an operator acting on registers $\alice \alice' \alice''$ (resp. $\bob \bob' \bob''$).
